lead: The bending equation gives the stress at every fibre, but design needs only the worst fibre. Section modulus packs the geometry into one number: Z = I/y_max, in mm³. The moment a section can carry is then M = σ Z, where σ is the allowable bending stress. A designer compares that against the bending moment diagram from Unit 3. The depth of a floor joist or the rolled steel beam over a platform is fixed by making Z large enough.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for centroid and I, 4.2 for M/I = σ/y = E/R, and Unit 3 for the bending moment diagram.

sections.h3: Stress varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis

blocks.text: Chapter 4.2 gave M/I = σ/y. Rearranged, σ = M y / I. Here σ is the bending stress at a fibre in N/mm² (the same as MPa), M is the bending moment at the section in N·mm, y is the distance of the fibre from the neutral axis in mm, and I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis in mm⁴.

The equation is linear in y. On the neutral axis y = 0, so σ = 0. Stress grows with distance, and the largest value sits on the extreme fibre at distance y_max. One fibre decides the strength of the whole section.
σ = M y / I     and     σ_max = M y_max / I
blocks.where: σ is the bending stress at distance y from the neutral axis (N/mm²); M is the bending moment at the section (N·mm); y is the distance of the fibre from the neutral axis (mm); I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis (mm⁴); y_max is the distance to the extreme fibre (mm); σ_max is the stress at that extreme fibre (N/mm²).

blocks.text: Draw it as a stress diagram: plot σ horizontally against y vertically. Two triangles meet at zero on the neutral axis, one in compression, one in tension, both peaking at the extreme fibres. The figure shows this for a 200 mm deep beam at 10 MPa extreme fibre stress.

Once M is known, the stress does not depend on the material. Two beams of the same section under the same moment carry the same bending stress whether steel or aluminium; only strain and curvature differ, through E.

sections.h3: Section modulus puts the geometry into one number

blocks.text: The designer needs only the worst fibre. Write σ_max = M y_max / I and group the geometry: Z = I / y_max, the section modulus in mm³. Then σ_max = M / Z, or M = σ Z. In this form M is the moment of resistance: the largest moment the section can take before the extreme fibre reaches the allowable stress σ.
Z = I / y_max     so     M = σ Z
blocks.where: Z is the section modulus (mm³); I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis (mm⁴); y_max is the distance from the neutral axis to the farthest fibre (mm); M is the moment of resistance (N·mm); σ is the allowable bending stress (N/mm²).

blocks.text: A 100 mm wide, 200 mm deep rectangle has Z = 100 × 200² / 6 = 666,666.67 mm³. Laid flat, 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep, Z = 200 × 100² / 6 = 333,333.33 mm³, exactly half. Depth enters as the square, width only linearly: doubling the depth quadruples Z and the moment capacity.

sections.h3: Unsymmetric sections have two section moduli

blocks.text: In a T-section, a channel, or an I-section with unequal flanges, the centroid is not at mid-depth, so y_top and y_bottom differ. Compute I about the centroidal axis, then Z_top = I / y_top and Z_bottom = I / y_bottom. Two section moduli, not one.

items: Find the centroid and put the neutral axis there (4.1).
Compute I about that centroidal axis, using the parallel axis theorem for each rectangle.
Measure y_top and y_bottom from the neutral axis, not from mid-depth. The larger is y_max.
If one allowable stress serves both tension and compression (mild steel), the smaller Z governs: M = σ I / y_max.
If the allowable stresses differ (cast iron is weak in tension), check each face: M_top = σ_top I / y_top and M_bottom = σ_bottom I / y_bottom. The smaller M is the moment of resistance.

blocks.text: Proportioning runs backwards: given M and σ, the required section modulus is Z = M / σ. Pick b and d so b d² / 6 reaches that value, then round to a standard size. A rectangular beam is usually two to three times deeper than it is wide, because depth buys capacity cheaply.

figure.caption: Bending stress against distance from the neutral axis for a 200 mm deep beam at 10 MPa extreme fibre stress. The line passes through zero at the neutral axis and reaches 10 MPa at the top and bottom fibres, 100 mm away.

spec.aria: Plot of bending stress against distance from the neutral axis for a 200 mm deep beam at 10 MPa extreme fibre stress; the line passes through zero at the neutral axis and is maximum at the top and bottom fibres.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 3 m carries a central point load W. Its cross-section is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. The allowable bending stress is 10 MPa. Find the safe load W. Neglect self weight.
steps: Moment of resistance: M = σ Z = 10 × 666,666.67 = 6,666,666.7 N·mm = 6.67 kN·m.
For a central point load on a simply supported span, the maximum moment is at midspan: M = W L / 4, with L = 3 m.
Check: σ = M / Z = 6,666,666.7 / 666,666.67 = 10 MPa, the allowable value.
examples.answer: The safe central load is W ≈ 8.89 kN.
examples.check:
b = 100.0
d = 200.0
L = 3.0
sigma = 10.0

I = b * d**3 / 12
y_max = d / 2
Z = I / y_max
M = sigma * Z / 1e6
W = 4 * M / L

print(f"Z = {Z:.2f} mm^3")
print(f"M = {M:.2f} kN m")
print(f"W = {W:.2f} kN")

traps: Using d/2 as y_max for an unsymmetric section. y_max is measured from the neutral axis, not mid-depth: a T-section can put the far fibre 120 mm from the neutral axis on a 160 mm deep shape.
Using b d² / 6 for bending about the weak axis without swapping b and d. The squared dimension must be the one in the plane of bending.
Mixing units. M in N·mm needs σ in N/mm² and Z in mm³. Feeding a moment in kN·m into M = σ Z is wrong by a factor of 10⁶.
Treating Z as a material property. It is pure geometry: same Z, same moment at the same stress, whether the steel is Fe 415 or Fe 500.
Taking the larger Z of an unsymmetric section when only one allowable stress is given. The farthest fibre reaches its limit first, so the smaller Z governs.

quiz.q: Define section modulus and state its units.
quiz.a: Z = I / y_max, where I is the second moment of area about the neutral axis and y_max is the distance from the neutral axis to the farthest fibre. Units: mm³.

quiz.q: Write the section modulus of a rectangle b × d and of a solid circle of diameter d.
quiz.a: Rectangle: Z = b d² / 6. Solid circle: Z = π d³ / 32.

quiz.q: Why is bending stress zero on the neutral axis and maximum at the extreme fibre?
quiz.a: σ = M y / I is proportional to y. Plane sections rotate about the neutral axis, so the fibre on it neither stretches nor shortens: zero strain, zero stress. The farthest fibre has the largest strain and, by Hooke's law, the largest stress.

quiz.q: Two 100 mm × 200 mm beams are used, one upright and one laid flat. Which carries more moment, and by what factor?
quiz.a: Upright: Z = 100 × 200² / 6 = 666,666.67 mm³. Flat: Z = 200 × 100² / 6 = 333,333.33 mm³. The upright beam carries twice the moment at the same stress, because depth enters squared.

quiz.q: A cantilever 2 m long has a section 60 mm wide and 120 mm deep. Allowable stress 8 MPa. Find the uniformly distributed load w over its full length. Neglect self weight.
quiz.a: Z = 60 × 120² / 6 = 144,000 mm³. M = σ Z = 8 × 144,000 = 1,152,000 N·mm = 1.152 kN·m. For a cantilever under UDL, M = w L² / 2 at the fixed end, so w = 2 M / L² = 2 × 1.152 / 4 = 0.576 kN/m.

quiz.q: A hollow circular beam has outside diameter 200 mm and inside diameter 120 mm, with 12 MPa allowable stress. Find its moment of resistance.

A T-section has I = 3.2×10⁷ mm⁴ about the neutral axis, top fibre 40 mm and bottom fibre 120 mm from it. (a) Mild steel, 10 MPa allowed in both tension and compression. (b) Cast iron, 10 MPa compression at top and 3 MPa tension at bottom. Find the moment of resistance in each case and say which face governs in (b).
quiz.a: (a) The far fibre is the bottom, y_max = 120 mm. Z = 3.2×10⁷ / 120 = 266,666.67 mm³. M = 10 × 266,666.67 ≈ 2.67 kN·m. (b) Top: M = 10 × 3.2×10⁷ / 40 = 8.0 kN·m. Bottom: M = 3 × 3.2×10⁷ / 120 = 0.80 kN·m. The tension face governs, so M = 0.80 kN·m.

quiz.q: A rectangular beam of width b and depth d is replaced by one of the same width and twice the depth. What happens to Z, to I, and to the deflection under the same load?
quiz.a: Z = b d² / 6 rises 4 times, so the moment capacity at the same allowable stress rises 4 times. I = b d³ / 12 rises 8 times. Deflection varies as 1 / I, so it falls to one-eighth.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real codes go past the elastic section modulus. Steel design uses a plastic section modulus Z_p, and the ratio Z_p / Z is the shape factor: about 1.5 for a rectangle, about 1.14 for an I-section. Indian limit state steel design works with these plastic values, so the elastic Z here is the first step, not the last. Rolled steel tables list Z for every standard ISMB and ISMC shape, which is why designers rarely integrate by hand. Look up 'plastic section modulus', 'shape factor' and 'limit state design of steel beams'.
